newsitem.title: UK: Mark firm, but mostly unresponsive to Europe news.
newsitem.headline: Mark firm, but mostly unresponsive to Europe news.

text.p: The mark was firm against other European currencies in late trade but moves were not large, with traders saying the market was exhausted after being inundated by news about monetary union all week.
The mark twitched lower after the German finance ministry and the Bundesbank reached an agreement on revaluing the central bank's currency reserves, but it soon recovered.

Meanwhile, French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's policy speech, which traders had hoped would provide some hints on the new French adminstration's commitment to Europe's monetary union, was devoid of market-moving factors.
"There were times today when some of them (European currencies) looked set to get moving, but it never really happened," said Itsuro Karasawa, assistant general manager at Sakura Bank in London.
"With the EU summit (earlier this week) over and out of the way the market is feeling comfortable about EMU, and there isn't much speculation about that right now," he said.

The mark was at 3.3751/54 French francs at 1520 GMT against 3.3742/47 in late trade on Wednesday. Against the lira, it was at 979.55/85 against 979.70/90. Both had been trading in very narrow ranges throughout the day.

Analysts said the agreement concerning the Bundesbank's reserves evoked a knee-jerk reaction from the market in that it alleviated a row between Bonn and the Bundesbank over tapping the central bank reserves in its bid to qualify for EMU.

The central bank said it would carry out a valuation close to market prices and retain the principle of lowest value, with German coalition sources saying the Buba's dollar reserves would be assessed at at least 1.50 marks.
But the impact on the mark crosses was minimal and fleeting.
"That (the use of Buba reserves) was never going to be a big money-spinner," said Francis Breedon, forex analyst at Lehman.
"The issue was interesting because of the conflict it caused (between the Bundesbank and the government), which was resolved some time ago," Breedon said.
Meanwhile, Jospin's speech failed to move the market because although he reaffirmed his commitment to achieving EMU on time, he steered clear of specifics concerning the single currency.
"It wasn't as exciting as it might have been because Jospin didn't have the numbers (about budget deficits) and the details we need to know," Lehman's Breedon said.
